title: Engineering Dynamics

sources.title: UCL module catalogue: MECH0006 Engineering Dynamics (2026/27)
sources.used_for: aims, ordered topic list, learning outcomes, credits, term and assessment for 2026/27

about: Engineering Dynamics (MECH0006) is a 15-credit, Term 2 module in UCL's Department of Mechanical Engineering that introduces classical mechanics in an engineering context and builds systematic problem-solving skills. Its 2026/27 catalogue entry lists six topics in order, which this pack follows: particle kinematics, then particle kinetics by Newton's laws and by work–energy and impulse–momentum, then the same three steps for rigid bodies in plane motion. It is taught in person and, for 2026/27, assessed by an exam (70%) and coursework (30%). Numerical examples here use g = 9.81 m/s².
topics: Kinetics of particles: Newton's laws of motion
Kinetics of particles: work-energy and impulse-momentum
Kinetics of rigid bodies: Newton's laws of motion
Kinetics of rigid bodies: work-energy and impulse-momentum

notes.body:
Kinematics describes motion (position, velocity, acceleration) without asking what causes it. A particle is a body whose size and rotation do not matter for the problem, so it can be treated as a point. Use g = 9.81 m/s² unless told otherwise.

Rectilinear motion
- Velocity v = ds/dt; acceleration a = dv/dt = v dv/ds.
- The form a = v dv/ds is the one to reach for when acceleration is given as a function of position (springs, drag that depends on distance).
- For constant acceleration only: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as. Do not use these when a varies; integrate instead.
- Graphs: the slope of an s–t graph is v, the slope of a v–t graph is a, and the area under a v–t graph is displacement.

Curvilinear motion: choose the coordinate system that suits the problem
- Rectangular (x–y): best for projectiles. With no air resistance, aₓ = 0 and a_y = −g, so the two directions are solved separately and linked only by time.
- Normal–tangential (n–t): best when the path is known (a road curve, a track). The tangential component aₜ = dv/dt changes the speed; the normal component aₙ = v²/ρ points towards the centre of curvature and changes the direction. Total a = √(aₜ² + aₙ²).
- Polar (r–θ): best when motion is described by a distance and an angle from a fixed point (a slider on a rotating arm, a radar tracking problem). vᵣ = ṙ, v_θ = rθ̇; aᵣ = r̈ − rθ̇², a_θ = rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇. The term 2ṙθ̇ is the Coriolis component and is the one most often forgotten.

Projectile results (launch speed u at angle α above horizontal, landing at launch height)
- Time of flight = 2u sin α / g; range = u² sin 2α / g; maximum height = (u sin α)² / (2g).
- Worked example: u = 20 m/s, α = 30°. Time of flight = 2 × 20 × 0.5 / 9.81 = 2.04 s; range = 400 × sin 60° / 9.81 = 35.3 m; maximum height = 10² / 19.62 = 5.10 m.
- These formulae only hold when the landing point is at the launch height. For a cliff or a target at a different height, write x(t) and y(t) and solve.

Worked n–t example
A car travels at 20 m/s around a bend of radius 100 m while braking at 3 m/s². aₙ = 20²/100 = 4 m/s² towards the centre, aₜ = 3 m/s² opposite to the velocity. The magnitude is √(4² + 3²) = 5 m/s². The two components are perpendicular, so they combine by Pythagoras, never by simple addition.

Relative motion
- r_B = r_A + r_B/A, so v_B = v_A + v_B/A and a_B = a_A + a_B/A (for translating axes).
- Draw a vector triangle: many exam questions are "what does a passenger in car A see car B doing?".

Dependent motion
- For pulley systems, write the total rope length as a sum of position coordinates and differentiate: the constant length gives relations between velocities and accelerations (for example, a block hanging from a movable pulley moves at half the speed of the free rope end).

Exam tips: state your sign convention and origin first; check which coordinate system makes the geometry easiest; only use constant-acceleration formulae when a really is constant; and give vectors with both magnitude and direction.

Kinetics links motion to the forces that cause it. For a particle of constant mass, Newton's second law is ΣF = ma, a vector equation that gives one scalar equation per direction.

Newton's three laws
- First law: a particle stays at rest or moves at constant velocity unless a net force acts on it.
- Second law: ΣF = ma, measured in an inertial (non-accelerating) frame.
- Third law: the forces two bodies exert on each other are equal in size, opposite in direction and collinear. They act on different bodies, so they never cancel within one free-body diagram.

The standard method
1. Draw a free-body diagram (FBD) of each body: every force acting on it, and nothing else.
2. Draw a kinetic diagram alongside showing ma (the "effective force").
3. Choose axes that match the motion: along and perpendicular to an incline, or n–t for curved paths, or polar.
4. Write ΣF = ma in each direction, add kinematic constraints (string lengths, rolling, contact), then solve.

Friction
- Static friction can take any value up to μₛN; it only reaches μₛN when slip is about to happen.
- Once sliding, kinetic friction is μₖN, opposing the relative sliding velocity.
- N is found from the equation perpendicular to the surface; it is not always mg.

Worked example: block on a rough incline
A block slides down a 30° slope with μₖ = 0.2. Perpendicular to the slope: N = mg cos 30°. Along the slope: ma = mg sin 30° − μₖmg cos 30°. So a = 9.81(0.5 − 0.2 × 0.866) = 3.21 m/s². The mass cancels.

Worked example: connected particles (Atwood machine)
Masses of 5 kg and 3 kg hang either side of a light, frictionless pulley on a light, inextensible string.
- 5 kg: 5g − T = 5a
- 3 kg: T − 3g = 3a
- Adding: a = (5 − 3)g/8 = 2.45 m/s². Then T = 3(g + a) = 36.8 N.
- T lies between the two weights (29.4 N and 49.1 N), which is a good sense check.

Curved paths (n–t form)
- ΣFₙ = mv²/ρ (towards the centre) and ΣFₜ = m dv/dt.
- Flat curve with friction: the maximum speed without skidding is v = √(μₛgr). For μₛ = 0.6 and r = 50 m, v = √(0.6 × 9.81 × 50) = 17.2 m/s.
- Banked curve without friction: the design speed satisfies tan θ = v²/(gr), and the normal reaction is N = mg/cos θ.
- "Centrifugal force" is not a real force in an inertial frame. On an FBD, the inward net force provides mv²/ρ.

Variable forces
- If the force depends on position (spring F = −kx), use a = v dv/dx and integrate.
- If it depends on velocity (drag), use a = dv/dt and separate variables.

Exam tips: a clear FBD earns method marks even if your algebra slips. Check signs by asking which way the body actually accelerates, and check limiting cases (μ = 0, equal masses).

Newton's second law can be integrated in two useful ways. Integrating over distance gives the work–energy principle; integrating over time gives the impulse–momentum principle. Each removes the need to find the acceleration.

Work and kinetic energy
- Work done by a force: U = ∫F · dr. Only the component of force along the displacement does work. A constant force F at angle θ to a straight displacement s does U = Fs cos θ.
- Kinetic energy T = ½mv².
- Work–energy principle: T₁ + ΣU₁→₂ = T₂.
- Normal reactions on a fixed surface and the tension in a pivoted pendulum string do no work, because they are perpendicular to the motion.

Conservative forces and potential energy
- Gravity: V_g = mgh (h measured upwards from a datum you choose).
- Linear spring: V_e = ½kx², where x is the extension or compression from the natural length (always positive energy).
- If only conservative forces do work: T₁ + V₁ = T₂ + V₂. Friction is non-conservative; include it as work done (−μₖN × distance).

Worked example: spring buffer
A 2 kg block moving at 4 m/s on a smooth surface hits a spring of stiffness 800 N/m. At maximum compression the block is momentarily at rest, so ½mv² = ½kx²: 16 = 400x², giving x = 0.200 m.

Power and efficiency
- Power P = dU/dt = F · v (units W).
- Efficiency η = output power / input power, always less than 1 for real machines.

Impulse and momentum
- Linear momentum L = mv. Impulse of a force = ∫F dt (area under the F–t graph).
- Impulse–momentum: mv₁ + Σ∫F dt = mv₂ (a vector equation).
- If the net external impulse on a system is zero in some direction, momentum is conserved in that direction. Internal forces (such as the contact force during a collision) cancel in pairs.

Impact and coefficient of restitution
- For direct central impact: momentum is conserved, m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
- Coefficient of restitution e = (v₂ − v₁)/(u₁ − u₂), the speed of separation divided by the speed of approach. e = 1 is perfectly elastic (no kinetic energy lost); e = 0 is perfectly plastic (the bodies move off together).
- Worked example: 2 kg at 6 m/s hits a stationary 3 kg block, e = 0.5. Momentum: 12 = 2v₁ + 3v₂. Restitution: v₂ − v₁ = 3. So v₁ = 0.6 m/s and v₂ = 3.6 m/s. Kinetic energy falls from 36 J to 19.8 J, a loss of 16.2 J.

Angular momentum of a particle
- H_O = r × mv. The moment of the forces about O equals dH_O/dt. If the net moment about O is zero (central forces, a ball on a string pulled through a hole), H_O is conserved.

Choosing a method
- Forces and positions known, speed wanted: work–energy.
- Forces and times known, or collisions: impulse–momentum.
- Acceleration or forces at an instant: Newton's second law.

Exam tips: state which principle you are using; in collisions, write the momentum and restitution equations with one consistent sign convention; never assume kinetic energy is conserved in an impact unless e = 1.

A rigid body has size and can rotate, so we need angular as well as linear quantities. In this module the focus is plane motion: every point moves in a plane parallel to a fixed reference plane.

Types of plane motion
- Translation: every line in the body keeps its orientation; all points share the same velocity and acceleration.
- Rotation about a fixed axis: every point moves in a circle about the axis.
- General plane motion: a combination of translation and rotation (a rolling wheel, a connecting rod).

Rotation about a fixed axis
- Angular position θ, angular velocity ω = dθ/dt, angular acceleration α = dω/dt (all the same for every point on the body).
- Constant α: ω = ω₀ + αt, θ = ω₀t + ½αt², ω² = ω₀² + 2αθ.
- A point at radius r: v = ωr, aₜ = αr, aₙ = ω²r (towards the axis).
- Worked example: a flywheel goes from rest to 1200 rpm in 8 s with constant α. ω = 1200 × 2π/60 = 125.7 rad/s, α = 15.7 rad/s², and θ = ½αt² = 502.7 rad = 80 revolutions.
- Belts and meshing gears: the contact point has the same speed on both, so ω_A r_A = ω_B r_B.

Relative velocity in general plane motion
- For two points A and B on the same body: v_B = v_A + ω × r_B/A.
- The relative term has size ωr_B/A and is perpendicular to the line AB. This is the key idea: relative to A, B can only move in a circle.
- In 2D, ω × r with ω = ωk and r = (x, y) gives (−ωy, ωx).

Instantaneous centre of zero velocity (IC)
- At any instant there is a point (on or off the body) with zero velocity; the body is momentarily rotating about it, so every point has speed ω × (distance to IC), perpendicular to the line from the IC.
- To find it: draw lines perpendicular to the known velocity directions of two points; they meet at the IC.
- The IC has zero velocity but generally not zero acceleration, so it cannot be used for accelerations.

Worked example: sliding rod
A 1 m rod has end A on the floor moving at 2 m/s and end B on a vertical wall; the rod makes 60° with the floor. The IC is where the vertical through A meets the horizontal through B. Its distance from A is L sin 60° = 0.866 m, so ω = 2/0.866 = 2.31 rad/s. Its distance from B is L cos 60° = 0.5 m, so v_B = 2.31 × 0.5 = 1.15 m/s (downwards).

Rolling without slipping
- The contact point has zero velocity, so v_G = ωr and a_G = αr (on a flat surface).
- A wheel of radius 0.3 m rolling at 6 m/s has ω = 20 rad/s; the top point moves at 12 m/s and a point level with the centre at 6√2 = 8.49 m/s at 45°.

Relative acceleration
- a_B = a_A + α × r_B/A − ω²r_B/A. The last term points from B towards A.
- Solve as a vector equation, usually by resolving into i and j components; two unknowns (for example α and one acceleration) can be found.

Exam tips: always sketch the velocity directions you know; find ω first (the IC is often fastest), then the velocities you need; use the vector relative-acceleration equation for accelerations.

For a rigid body in plane motion, Newton's laws give three scalar equations: two for the translation of the centre of mass G and one for rotation.

Equations of motion
- ΣFₓ = m a_Gx and ΣF_y = m a_Gy (the centre of mass moves as if all the mass and force were concentrated there).
- ΣM_G = I_G α (moments taken about G).
- For rotation about a fixed axis through O: ΣM_O = I_O α, which avoids finding the pin reaction.
- More generally, ΣM_P = I_G α + (moment of m a_G about P): the "kinetic moment". This lets you take moments about a convenient point such as a contact point.

Mass moment of inertia
- I = ∫r² dm (units kg m²); it measures resistance to angular acceleration, just as mass resists linear acceleration.
- Standard results (uniform bodies, mass m): slender rod about its centre mL²/12, about one end mL²/3; solid disc or cylinder about its axis ½mr²; thin ring or hoop mr²; solid sphere about a diameter ⅖mr².
- Parallel axis theorem: I = I_G + md², where d is the distance between the parallel axes. Only valid when one axis passes through G.
- Radius of gyration k: I = mk².

Worked example: rod released from horizontal
A uniform 6 kg rod of length 2 m is pinned at one end and released from rest horizontally.
- I_O = mL²/3 = 8 kg m². Moment of weight about O = mg × L/2 = 58.9 N m.
- α = (mgL/2)/(mL²/3) = 3g/(2L) = 7.36 rad/s².
- a_G = α × L/2 = 7.36 m/s² downwards (ω = 0, so no normal component).
- Vertical equation: mg − R = m a_G, so R = 6(9.81 − 7.36) = 14.7 N, exactly mg/4. The pin carries much less than the weight at the instant of release.

Worked example: drum and hanging mass
A 4 kg mass hangs from a cord wrapped round a uniform 10 kg disc of radius 0.2 m on a frictionless axle (I = ½MR² = 0.2 kg m²).
- Mass: mg − T = ma. Drum: TR = Iα, with a = αR (cord does not slip).
- So a = mg/(m + I/R²) = 39.24/(4 + 5) = 4.36 m/s², T = 4(9.81 − 4.36) = 21.8 N, α = 21.8 rad/s².

Rolling down an incline
- For a body rolling without slipping, a_G = g sin θ/(1 + k²/r²).
- Solid cylinder: ⅔g sin θ; solid sphere: 5/7 g sin θ; hoop: ½g sin θ. The friction needed is F = m g sin θ − m a_G; rolling requires F ≤ μₛN.

Method
1. FBD and kinetic diagram (m a_G at G and I_G α as a couple).
2. Kinematic constraints (a = αr, rolling, pinned point).
3. Three equations, solve, check signs and units.

Exam tips: list I for each body before starting; take moments about a fixed pivot or the point where unknown forces act to shorten the algebra; remember ΣM_G = I_G α holds only about G (or a fixed axis), unless you include the moment of m a_G.

notes.h: Rigid body energy and momentum methods
notes.body:
The energy and momentum principles from particle kinetics extend to rigid bodies once rotation is included. They are often much quicker than Newton's laws when you want a speed after a displacement or after an impact.

Kinetic energy of a rigid body
- Translation only: T = ½m v_G².
- Fixed-axis rotation about O: T = ½I_O ω².
- General plane motion: T = ½m v_G² + ½I_G ω². (Equivalently ½I_IC ω² about the instantaneous centre.)

Work in rigid body problems
- Forces: U = ∫F · dr, as for particles.
- A couple M turning through angle θ does work U = Mθ (constant M).
- Forces that do no work: pin reactions at a fixed pivot; the normal reaction and the friction force at the contact point of a body rolling without slipping (the contact point has zero velocity).

Conservation of energy
- T₁ + V₁ = T₂ + V₂ when only conservative forces do work. Gravity potential uses the height of G.
- Worked example: a 6 kg, 2 m rod pinned at one end swings down from horizontal. G drops L/2 = 1 m, so mg(L/2) = ½(mL²/3)ω², giving ω = √(3g/L) = 3.84 rad/s at the vertical. The free end moves at ωL = 7.67 m/s, faster than a particle dropped through 2 m (6.26 m/s).
- Worked example: a solid cylinder rolls from rest down a height h. mgh = ½mv² + ½(½mr²)(v/r)² = ¾mv², so v = √(4gh/3). For h = 2 m, v = 5.11 m/s. One third of its kinetic energy is rotational.

Linear and angular momentum
- Linear momentum: L = m v_G. Impulse–momentum: m v_G1 + Σ∫F dt = m v_G2.
- Angular momentum about G: H_G = I_G ω. About a fixed axis O: H_O = I_O ω.
- Angular impulse–momentum: I_O ω₁ + Σ∫M_O dt = I_O ω₂. Example: a constant torque of 12 N m for 3 s on a 4 kg m² flywheel from rest gives ω = 36/4 = 9 rad/s.

Conservation of angular momentum
- If the net external moment about an axis is zero, angular momentum about that axis is conserved, even if kinetic energy is not.
- Worked example: a disc (I₁ = 0.5 kg m²) spins at 10 rad/s; a second disc (I₂ = 0.3 kg m²), initially at rest, is dropped onto it coaxially and they lock together. 0.5 × 10 = 0.8ω, so ω = 6.25 rad/s. Kinetic energy drops from 25 J to 15.6 J; 9.4 J is dissipated by friction between the discs.
- Ice skaters, divers and rotating machinery with sliding masses use the same idea: decreasing I increases ω.

Eccentric impact (introductory)
- When a body pivoted at O is struck, take angular momentum about O: the large pin impulse then has no moment and drops out.

Exam tips: write T for every body in the system, including rotation; choose the datum for V and state it; in impacts use momentum (linear or angular) first, never energy, unless the impact is stated to be elastic.

cards.b: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as. Valid only when acceleration is constant; otherwise integrate a = dv/dt or a = v dv/ds.

cards.f: a = v dv/ds: when to use it
cards.b: When acceleration is given as a function of position, e.g. a = −kx. Separate variables: ∫v dv = ∫a ds.
aₜ = dv/dt along the path (changes speed); aₙ = v²/ρ towards the centre of curvature (changes direction). Magnitude a = √(aₜ² + aₙ²).
aᵣ = r̈ − rθ̇² and a_θ = rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇. The 2ṙθ̇ term (Coriolis) appears whenever r and θ both change.
R = u² sin 2α / g, maximum at α = 45° (no air resistance, landing at launch height).
Horizontal: constant velocity (aₓ = 0). Vertical: constant acceleration −g. The two are linked only through time.
v_B = v_A + v_B/A: B's velocity equals A's velocity plus B's velocity as seen by a (non-rotating) observer moving with A.
Displacement over that time interval; the gradient of the v–t graph is acceleration.
ΣF = ma, valid in an inertial frame for constant mass; resolve into one scalar equation per direction.
Equal, opposite, collinear forces acting on two different bodies, so they never appear on the same free-body diagram.
Takes whatever value (up to μₛN) is needed to prevent slipping; equals μₛN only when slip is about to occur.
F = μₖN, opposing the direction of relative sliding. Find N from the force balance perpendicular to the surface.

cards.f: Maximum speed on a flat curve
cards.b: v = √(μₛgr): friction is the only horizontal force, so μₛmg = mv²/r.
tan θ = v²/(gr); normal reaction N = mg/cos θ.
a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂) for light frictionless pulley and string; T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂).
A sketch showing the ma vector(s) next to the free-body diagram, so ΣF on one side equals ma on the other.
T₁ + ΣU₁→₂ = T₂, where T = ½mv². Forces perpendicular to the motion do no work.

cards.f: Elastic potential energy of a spring
cards.b: V = ½kx², with x the extension or compression from the natural length.
T₁ + V₁ = T₂ + V₂, valid when only conservative forces (gravity, springs) do work.
mv₁ + Σ∫F dt = mv₂. Impulse is the area under the force–time graph.
e = (v₂ − v₁)/(u₁ − u₂), separation speed over approach speed along the line of impact; 0 ≤ e ≤ 1.
e = 0: bodies move off together; momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is lost.
P = F · v (rate of doing work), in watts. Efficiency = output power / input power.

cards.f: Conservation of angular momentum of a particle
cards.b: If the net moment about O is zero, H_O = r × mv stays constant (e.g. central-force motion).

cards.f: Fixed-axis rotation: point velocity and acceleration
cards.b: v = ωr, aₜ = αr, aₙ = ω²r towards the axis.
Multiply by 2π/60: 1200 rpm = 125.7 rad/s.

cards.f: Relative velocity on a rigid body
cards.b: v_B = v_A + ω × r_B/A; the relative term has size ωr_B/A and is perpendicular to AB.
Point with zero velocity at that instant; found where perpendiculars to two known velocity directions meet. Each point's speed = ω × distance from IC.

cards.f: Can the IC be used for accelerations?
cards.b: No: the IC has zero velocity but in general a non-zero acceleration.
Contact point is at rest: v_G = ωr and a_G = αr. Top of the wheel moves at 2v_G.

cards.f: Relative acceleration on a rigid body
cards.b: a_B = a_A + α × r_B/A − ω²r_B/A; the ω² term points from B towards A.
Contact points share the same speed: ω_A r_A = ω_B r_B.

cards.f: Plane motion equations for a rigid body
cards.b: ΣFₓ = m a_Gx, ΣF_y = m a_Gy, ΣM_G = I_G α.
I = I_G + md², with d the distance from G's axis to the parallel axis.
About centre: mL²/12. About one end: mL²/3 (= mL²/12 + m(L/2)²).
Disc/solid cylinder ½mr²; thin hoop mr²; solid sphere ⅖mr² (about axes through G).
k such that I = mk²: the radius at which all the mass could sit to give the same I.

cards.f: Rod pinned at one end released from horizontal
cards.b: α = 3g/(2L), a_G = 3g/4, pin reaction = mg/4 at release.
a_G = g sin θ/(1 + k²/r²): cylinder ⅔g sin θ, sphere 5/7 g sin θ, hoop ½g sin θ.
ΣM_O = I_O α about the fixed pivot removes the unknown pin reactions from the moment equation.

cards.f: Kinetic energy in general plane motion
cards.b: T = ½m v_G² + ½I_G ω² (or ½I_O ω² for fixed-axis rotation about O).

cards.f: Work done by a constant couple
cards.b: U = Mθ, with θ in radians.

cards.f: Forces that do no work on a rolling wheel
cards.b: Normal reaction and static friction at the contact point (no slipping), because that point has zero velocity.

cards.f: Rolling cylinder speed after height drop h
cards.b: v = √(4gh/3) from mgh = ¾mv²; a third of its kinetic energy is rotational.
I_O ω₁ + Σ∫M_O dt = I_O ω₂.
If the net external moment about an axis is zero, Iω about that axis is constant; kinetic energy may still be lost.

cards.f: Rod swinging from horizontal to vertical
cards.b: ω = √(3g/L) at the vertical (pinned at one end, released from rest).

cards.f: Eccentric impact: which point for moments?
cards.b: Take angular momentum about the fixed pivot so the unknown impulsive pin reaction has no moment.

questions.q: A car travels at 20 m/s round a bend of radius 100 m while braking at 3 m/s². What is the magnitude of its acceleration?
questions.why: The normal component is v²/ρ = 400/100 = 4 m/s² and the tangential component is 3 m/s²; they are perpendicular, so the magnitude is √(4² + 3²) = 5 m/s². 4 m/s² is the normal (centripetal) part alone, ignoring the braking. 3 m/s² is the braking alone, ignoring the curvature. 7 m/s² comes from adding the two components as scalars, which is wrong because they act at right angles.

questions.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 15 m/s. Ignoring air resistance (g = 9.81 m/s²), how high does it rise?
questions.why: At the top v = 0, so 0 = 15² − 2gh gives h = 225/19.62 = 11.5 m. 22.9 m is v²/g, which drops the factor of 2. 1.53 m is the number 15/9.81, which is the time to the top in seconds, not a height. 45.9 m comes from ½gt² using the whole time of flight (3.06 s) instead of the time to the top.

questions.q: A stone is thrown horizontally at 15 m/s from the top of a cliff 20 m high. Ignoring air resistance and taking g = 9.81 m/s², find (a) the time to reach the sea below, (b) the horizontal distance travelled, and (c) the speed and direction of the stone as it hits the water.
markScheme: Vertical motion from rest: 20 = ½ × 9.81 × t², so t = 2.02 s (1 mark)
Horizontal distance x = 15 × 2.02 = 30.3 m (1 mark)
Vertical velocity at impact = gt = 19.8 m/s; horizontal component stays 15 m/s (1 mark)
Direction: tan⁻¹(19.8/15) = 52.9° below the horizontal (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: Take x horizontal and y vertically downwards from the launch point. The initial vertical velocity is zero, so y = ½gt²: 20 = 4.905t², giving t = √(20/4.905) = 2.02 s. Horizontally there is no acceleration, so x = 15 × 2.02 = 30.3 m. At impact the vertical velocity is gt = 9.81 × 2.02 = 19.8 m/s downwards and the horizontal velocity is still 15 m/s. The speed is √(15² + 19.8²) = 24.8 m/s, directed at tan⁻¹(19.8/15) = 52.9° below the horizontal. (Check by energy: v² = 15² + 2 × 9.81 × 20 = 617.4, so v = 24.8 m/s.)

questions.q: Masses of 5 kg and 3 kg hang from either end of a light inextensible string over a light frictionless pulley and are released from rest. What is the tension in the string? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
questions.why: Writing ΣF = ma for each mass gives a = 2g/8 = 2.45 m/s², and T = 3(g + a) = 36.8 N. 49.1 N is the weight of the 5 kg mass, which would be the tension only if that mass were held at rest; because it accelerates downwards, the tension must be less than its weight. 29.4 N is the weight of the 3 kg mass, which ignores the upward acceleration of that mass. 22.1 N is 3(g − a), which gets the sign of the 3 kg mass's acceleration wrong: that mass accelerates upwards, so the tension must exceed its weight.

questions.q: A block slides down a 30° incline with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.2. What is its acceleration? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
questions.why: Along the slope a = g(sin 30° − μ cos 30°) = 9.81(0.5 − 0.173) = 3.21 m/s². 4.91 m/s² is g sin 30°, which ignores friction entirely. 6.60 m/s² adds the friction term, which treats friction as helping the motion rather than opposing it. 3.92 m/s² uses μ sin 30° for the friction term, i.e. it takes the normal reaction as mg sin 30° instead of mg cos 30°.

questions.q: A road bend of radius 80 m is banked at 15°. (a) Find the speed at which a car can take the bend with no tendency to slip (no friction needed). (b) For a 1200 kg car at that speed, find the normal reaction from the road. (g = 9.81 m/s²)
markScheme: Correct FBD: weight mg down, normal reaction N perpendicular to the road; acceleration v²/r horizontally towards the centre (1 mark)
Vertical: N cos θ = mg; horizontal: N sin θ = mv²/r, so tan θ = v²/(gr) (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: With no friction, only weight and the normal reaction act. The car moves in a horizontal circle, so its acceleration v²/r is horizontal, towards the centre. Vertically there is no acceleration: N cos 15° = mg. Horizontally: N sin 15° = mv²/r. Dividing, tan 15° = v²/(gr), so v = √(9.81 × 80 × 0.268) = 14.5 m/s, about 52 km/h. The normal reaction is N = mg/cos 15° = 11 772/0.966 = 12.2 kN, which is larger than the car's weight because N must also supply the horizontal component.

questions.q: A 2 kg block moving at 6 m/s strikes a stationary 3 kg block head-on. The coefficient of restitution is 0.5. What is the speed of the 3 kg block just after impact?
questions.why: Momentum gives 12 = 2v₁ + 3v₂ and restitution gives v₂ − v₁ = 0.5 × 6 = 3, so v₁ = 0.6 m/s and v₂ = 3.6 m/s. 2.4 m/s is the common speed for a perfectly plastic impact (e = 0). 4.8 m/s is the result for a perfectly elastic impact (e = 1). 4.0 m/s comes from assuming the 2 kg block stops dead, so all 12 kg m/s of momentum goes into the 3 kg block, which ignores the restitution condition.

questions.q: A 2 kg block moving at 4 m/s on a smooth surface compresses a spring of stiffness 800 N/m. What is the maximum compression?
questions.why: At maximum compression all kinetic energy is stored in the spring: ½ × 2 × 4² = ½ × 800 × x², so x² = 0.04 and x = 0.200 m. 0.141 m comes from writing the spring energy as kx² (missing its ½). 0.283 m comes from writing the kinetic energy as mv² (missing its ½). 0.020 m comes from dividing the kinetic energy (16 J) by k, which confuses energy with force and is dimensionally wrong.

questions.q: A 0.15 kg cricket ball arrives horizontally at 30 m/s and is struck straight back at 40 m/s. Contact lasts 2 ms. Find (a) the impulse on the ball and (b) the average force on it.
markScheme: Choose a sign convention: take the return direction as positive, so the initial velocity is −30 m/s (1 mark)
Impulse = m(v₂ − v₁) = 0.15 × (40 − (−30)) = 10.5 N s in the return direction (2 marks; 1 mark only if 1.5 N s from ignoring the reversal)
Average force = impulse / time = 10.5 / 0.002 = 5250 N (5.25 kN) (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: Take the direction the ball leaves the bat as positive. Its velocity changes from −30 m/s to +40 m/s, a change of 70 m/s. The impulse equals the change in momentum: 0.15 × 70 = 10.5 N s, directed back towards the bowler. The average force over 2 ms is 10.5/0.002 = 5250 N. A common error is to use 40 − 30 = 10 m/s, which forgets that the velocity reverses direction.

questions.q: A wheel of radius 0.3 m rolls without slipping along level ground with its centre moving at 6 m/s. What is the speed of the point at the top of the wheel?
questions.why: The contact point is the instantaneous centre, so ω = 6/0.3 = 20 rad/s and the top, 0.6 m from the IC, moves at 20 × 0.6 = 12 m/s. 6 m/s treats the wheel as if it were translating, ignoring rotation. 8.49 m/s (6√2) is the speed of a point level with the centre, 0.3√2 m from the IC. 0 m/s is the speed of the contact point at the bottom, not the top.

questions.q: A 1 m rod slides with end A on the floor and end B against a vertical wall. At the instant the rod makes 60° with the floor, A moves away from the wall at 2 m/s. What is the speed of B?
questions.why: The instantaneous centre is 0.866 m (L sin 60°) from A and 0.5 m (L cos 60°) from B, so ω = 2/0.866 = 2.31 rad/s and v_B = 2.31 × 0.5 = 1.15 m/s (equivalently v_B = v_A cot 60°). 2.00 m/s assumes both ends move at the same speed, which is only true at 45°. 3.46 m/s is v_A tan 60°, which inverts the ratio of distances from the IC. 1.00 m/s is v_A cos 60°, the component of A's velocity along the rod, wrongly taken as B's whole speed (B's velocity is vertical, so its component along the rod is v_B sin 60°, not v_B).

questions.q: A flywheel accelerates uniformly from rest to 1200 rpm in 8 s. Find (a) its angular acceleration, (b) the number of revolutions made in that time, and (c) the speed and normal (centripetal) acceleration of a point 0.25 m from the axis at t = 8 s.
markScheme: θ = ½αt² = 502.7 rad = 80 revolutions (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: Convert first: 1200 rpm = 1200 × 2π/60 = 125.7 rad/s. With uniform acceleration from rest, α = ω/t = 125.7/8 = 15.7 rad/s². The angle turned is θ = ½αt² = 0.5 × 15.7 × 64 = 502.7 rad, which is 502.7/2π = 80 revolutions (check: the average speed is 600 rpm for 8 s, i.e. 600 × 8/60 = 80 rev). At 8 s, a point at 0.25 m has v = ωr = 31.4 m/s and normal acceleration ω²r = 125.7² × 0.25 ≈ 3950 m/s² towards the axis; its tangential acceleration αr = 3.93 m/s² is tiny by comparison.

questions.q: A uniform rod of mass 6 kg and length 2 m is pinned at one end and released from rest in a horizontal position. What is its angular acceleration at the instant of release? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
questions.why: Taking moments about the pin: mg(L/2) = (mL²/3)α, so α = 3g/(2L) = 7.36 rad/s². 29.4 rad/s² uses I_G = mL²/12 instead of I about the pin, i.e. forgets the parallel axis term. 14.7 rad/s² uses the full length L as the moment arm of the weight instead of L/2. 9.81 rad/s² comes from assuming the centre of mass falls freely with a_G = g and then using α = a_G/(L/2) = g/1 m, which ignores the restraint of the pin.

questions.q: A 4 kg mass hangs from a cord wrapped around a uniform solid 10 kg disc of radius 0.2 m mounted on a frictionless horizontal axle. What is the acceleration of the mass?
questions.why: With I = ½MR² = 0.2 kg m², a = mg/(m + I/R²) = 39.24/(4 + 5) = 4.36 m/s². 9.81 m/s² ignores the disc altogether (free fall). 2.80 m/s² uses I = MR² as if the disc were a thin hoop. 7.85 m/s² comes from a = mgR²/I, which ignores the hanging mass's own inertia in the denominator.

questions.q: A 4 kg mass hangs from a light cord wrapped round a uniform solid disc (mass 10 kg, radius 0.2 m) that turns on a frictionless axle. The system is released from rest. Find the acceleration of the mass, the tension in the cord and the angular acceleration of the disc.
markScheme: I = ½MR² = 0.2 kg m² (1 mark)
Mass: mg − T = ma; disc: TR = Iα (1 mark)
Constraint a = αR (1 mark)
a = mg/(m + I/R²) = 4.36 m/s² (1 mark)
T = m(g − a) = 21.8 N and α = a/R = 21.8 rad/s² (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: The disc has I = ½ × 10 × 0.2² = 0.2 kg m². For the hanging mass (down positive): 4g − T = 4a. For the disc, the only moment about the axle is from the cord: T × 0.2 = 0.2α. The cord does not slip, so a = 0.2α. Substituting α = a/0.2 into the disc equation gives T = 0.2a/0.04 = 5a. Then 39.24 − 5a = 4a, so a = 4.36 m/s². The tension is T = 5a = 21.8 N, less than the weight of 39.2 N as expected, and α = 4.36/0.2 = 21.8 rad/s².

questions.q: A uniform solid cylinder is released from rest and rolls without slipping down a slope, descending a vertical height of 2 m. What is the speed of its centre at the bottom? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
questions.why: Energy: mgh = ½mv² + ½(½mr²)(v/r)² = ¾mv², so v = √(4gh/3) = 5.11 m/s. 6.26 m/s is √(2gh), which ignores rotational kinetic energy (a block sliding without friction). 4.43 m/s is √(gh), the result for a thin hoop with I = mr². 5.29 m/s is √(10gh/7), the result for a solid sphere with I = ⅖mr².

questions.q: A disc with I = 0.5 kg m² spins at 10 rad/s on a frictionless shaft. A second disc with I = 0.3 kg m², initially at rest, is dropped onto it coaxially and the two lock together. What is the final angular velocity?
questions.why: No external moment acts about the shaft, so angular momentum is conserved: 0.5 × 10 = (0.5 + 0.3)ω, so ω = 6.25 rad/s. 7.91 rad/s comes from conserving kinetic energy, but energy is dissipated as the discs grip each other, so energy is not conserved. 16.7 rad/s divides the initial angular momentum by the second disc's I alone, forgetting the first disc is still spinning. 10.0 rad/s assumes adding the second disc makes no difference, ignoring its inertia.

questions.q: A uniform solid cylinder of mass m and radius r is released from rest on a slope and rolls without slipping through a vertical drop of 2 m. (a) Find the speed of its centre at the bottom. (b) What fraction of its kinetic energy is rotational? (c) Explain why friction does no work.
markScheme: Energy equation mgh = ½mv² + ½I_G ω² with I_G = ½mr² and ω = v/r (1 mark)
¾mv² = mgh, so v = √(4gh/3) = 5.11 m/s (2 marks)
Rotational KE = ¼mv² out of ¾mv², so one third (1 mark)
Friction acts at the contact point, which has zero velocity when rolling without slipping, so it does no work (1 mark)
questions.modelAnswer: Gravity is the only force doing work. Rolling without slipping means ω = v/r. The kinetic energy at the bottom is ½mv² + ½(½mr²)(v/r)² = ½mv² + ¼mv² = ¾mv². Setting this equal to mgh = m × 9.81 × 2 gives v² = 4 × 9.81 × 2/3 = 26.2, so v = 5.11 m/s, independent of m and r. The rotational part is ¼mv² out of ¾mv², one third of the total. Friction is needed to make the cylinder spin, but it acts at the instantaneous contact point, whose velocity is zero, so its work is zero and mechanical energy is conserved.

questions.q:
Block A (mass 2 kg) is released from rest at the top of a smooth curved ramp, 1.25 m above a horizontal floor. At the bottom it slides onto the floor and immediately strikes block B (mass 3 kg), which is at rest. The coefficient of restitution between the blocks is 0.5. The floor is smooth up to B, but B then slides on a rough section with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.3. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
(a) Find the speed of A just before impact. [3]
(b) Find the velocities of A and B just after impact. [6]
(c) Find the kinetic energy lost in the impact. [3]
(d) Find how far B slides on the rough section before stopping. [4]
(e) If the impact lasts 5 ms, find the average force between the blocks. [4]
markScheme: (a) Energy conservation on the smooth ramp: v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.81 × 1.25) = 4.95 m/s
(b) Momentum equation 2 × 4.95 = 2v_A + 3v_B with a consistent sign convention
(b) Restitution equation v_B − v_A = 0.5 × 4.95 = 2.48 m/s; solve to give v_A = 0.495 m/s (still forwards) and v_B = 2.97 m/s
(c) KE before 24.5 J, after 0.245 + 13.24 = 13.5 J, loss ≈ 11.0 J
(d) Work–energy for B: ½ × 3 × 2.97² = 0.3 × 3 × 9.81 × d, giving d = v_B²/(2μg) = 1.50 m
(e) Impulse on B = 3 × 2.97 = 8.91 N s; average force = 8.91/0.005 ≈ 1.78 kN
Clear statement of which principle is used at each stage and why energy is not conserved in the impact
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The ramp is smooth, so mechanical energy is conserved: ½mv² = mgh gives v = √(2 × 9.81 × 1.25) = 4.95 m/s.

(b) Take the direction of A's motion as positive. During the very short impact, the only significant horizontal forces are the internal contact forces, so momentum is conserved: 2(4.95) = 2v_A + 3v_B, i.e. 9.90 = 2v_A + 3v_B. Restitution: v_B − v_A = e × (approach speed) = 0.5 × 4.95 = 2.48. Substituting v_B = v_A + 2.48: 9.90 = 5v_A + 7.43, so v_A = 0.495 m/s and v_B = 2.97 m/s. Both are positive: A carries on slowly in its original direction behind B.

(c) Before: ½ × 2 × 4.95² = 24.5 J (which also equals mgh = 2 × 9.81 × 1.25). After: ½ × 2 × 0.495² + ½ × 3 × 2.97² = 0.245 + 13.24 = 13.5 J. Loss ≈ 11.0 J, dissipated as heat, sound and permanent deformation because e < 1.

(d) On the rough section the normal reaction on B is 3g, so friction is 0.3 × 3 × 9.81 = 8.83 N. Work–energy: 0 = ½ × 3 × 2.97² − 8.83d, giving d = 13.24/8.83 = 1.50 m. (Equivalently d = v_B²/(2μg), independent of B's mass.)

(e) The impulse on B equals its change of momentum: 3 × 2.97 = 8.91 N s. Over 5 ms the average force is 8.91/0.005 = 1780 N, i.e. about 1.78 kN, roughly 60 times B's weight. This is why impulsive forces dominate during collisions and finite forces such as friction can be neglected while the impact lasts.

questions.q:
A uniform slender rod OA of mass 6 kg and length 2 m is pinned at O to a frictionless horizontal axle. It is held horizontal and released from rest. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
(a) Find the angular acceleration of the rod and the pin reaction at O immediately after release. [6]
(b) Find the angular velocity of the rod when it reaches the vertical position. [5]
(c) Find the pin reaction at O at the vertical position. [5]
(d) Compare the speed of end A at the vertical with the speed of a particle dropped from rest through the same height, and comment. [4]
markScheme: (a) I_O = mL²/3 = 8 kg m²; ΣM_O = I_O α gives α = 3g/(2L) = 7.36 rad/s²
(a) ω = 0 so a_G is purely tangential: a_G = α L/2 = 7.36 m/s² downwards; mg − R = m a_G gives R = mg/4 = 14.7 N upwards (no horizontal component since a_Gn = 0)
(b) Energy: G falls L/2 = 1 m; mg(L/2) = ½ I_O ω², so ω = √(3g/L) = 3.84 rad/s
(c) At the vertical the weight has no moment about O, so α = 0 and a_G = ω²(L/2) = 3g/2 = 14.7 m/s² upwards towards O
(c) R − mg = m a_G gives R = 2.5mg = 147 N upwards
(d) v_A = ωL = 7.67 m/s versus √(2gL) = 6.26 m/s for free fall through 2 m
(d) Comment: the rod's rotation transfers energy from the inner part to the tip; the end moves faster than free fall, while G moves slower
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) About the fixed pin, I_O = mL²/3 = 6 × 4/3 = 8 kg m². The weight acts at G, L/2 = 1 m from O, so ΣM_O = 6 × 9.81 × 1 = 58.9 N m. Then α = 58.9/8 = 7.36 rad/s² (= 3g/2L). At release ω = 0, so G has no normal acceleration and its acceleration is a_G = α × L/2 = 7.36 m/s² vertically downwards. Horizontally there is no acceleration, so the horizontal pin force is zero. Vertically: mg − R = m a_G, R = 6(9.81 − 7.36) = 14.7 N upwards, which is exactly mg/4.

(b) Only gravity does work (the pin is fixed and frictionless). Taking the datum at O, G falls 1 m: mg × 1 = ½ I_O ω², so 58.9 = 4ω², ω² = 14.7 and ω = 3.84 rad/s. This matches the formula ω = √(3g/L).

(c) At the vertical, the weight passes through O, so ΣM_O = 0 and α = 0. G therefore has only a normal acceleration towards O: a_G = ω² × L/2 = 14.7 × 1 = 14.7 m/s² upwards (equal to 3g/2). Vertically: R − mg = m a_G, so R = 6(9.81 + 14.7) = 147 N upwards. This is 2.5 times the weight, which is why pivots on swinging members must be designed for loads well above the static weight.

(d) The end A moves at v_A = ωL = 3.84 × 2 = 7.67 m/s. A particle falling freely through the same 2 m would reach √(2 × 9.81 × 2) = 6.26 m/s. The rod's tip is faster than free fall because the rod is rigid: the energy released by the whole rod (whose centre falls only 1 m) is shared by rotation, and points far from the pivot move faster than points near it. The centre G moves at ωL/2 = 3.84 m/s, slower than free fall through 1 m (4.43 m/s). This is the reason a falling chimney or tall tower can break: the upper part would need to accelerate faster than gravity alone can provide.
